title: Living water (John 4:7–15)
hookLine: whoever drinks the water I give shall not thirst for ever

lines: A WOMAN COMES TO DRAW WATER.
cards: Noon in Samaria, about the sixth hour, John says. Jesus is tired from the road and sits down by Jacob's well while his disciples go into the town to buy food. A woman of Samaria comes out with her jar to draw water.
John adds a note on the distance between them: the Jews do not communicate with the Samaritans. A Jewish man, a Samaritan woman, and a well between them. And his first words to her are a request.

teach.b: He says: "Give me to drink." In John's telling, the one with the gift begins by asking. She's startled: how do you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman?

He answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water."
Living water can mean plain running water: a spring, not still water in a cistern. She takes him that way, very practically. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep.
Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well? He doesn't argue about Jacob. He points at the bucket.
Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again.
But "he that shall drink of the water that I will give him, shall not thirst for ever." It becomes a spring inside, welling up into everlasting life.
And she answers like anyone carrying a heavy jar: Sir, give me this water, so I don't have to keep coming here. Early in its teaching on prayer, the Catechism turns to this scene.
Jesus thirsts, it says, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us.
Prayer, whether we know it or not, is the meeting of God's thirst with ours.

how: Catholics hear the woman at the well on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, often with adults preparing for baptism at Easter, and the Catechism turns to this scene early in its teaching on prayer.

games.q: you're a tired traveler at a well at noon. a Samaritan woman comes alone to draw water. Jews and Samaritans don't mix, John says. what do you do?
o: move to the other side of the well.
games.why: "Give me to drink." he asks first, and the conversation turns to living water.

practice: If you can, pour a glass of water, feel its weight, and take one slow sip, then another, noticing the cool of it going down.
Under this thirst, notice any deeper one: something you keep going back to the well for that never quite fills.
If you pray, ask as she did, give me this water; if not, just drink slowly and notice being thirsty, and being given something.

wordCard.voice: Living water. A phrase for running spring water; in John, the gift Jesus offers at Jacob's well that ends thirst for ever. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: living water (John 4:10), a phrase that can mean running, spring water.

carryVoice: Your line: never thirst. The one who asked for a drink is the one with the water. Five hundred days, done.
